_authoring: Every claim below is sourced from the resume, the project descriptions, or
credentials.json. Nothing has been inferred about motivation or feeling.
GAPS — only you can write these, and the page is built so it reads fine
without them. Add a chapter, or extend an existing `body`, when ready:
1. Why you started programming at all. The arc currently begins at
university because that is the first thing on record.
2. What you struggled with hardest, and how long it actually took. This
is the single most useful thing for a reader one step behind you.
3. A concrete moment something clicked — a bug, a concept, a project.
4. What you would tell someone in their first year now.
Resist adding a chapter you cannot make specific. A vague paragraph about
'passion for technology' is worse than one fewer chapter.
lede: I build systems for a living and explain them for the same reason I once needed them explained. This is the order things actually happened in — including the parts that took longer than they should have.

chapters.title: Learning the fundamentals properly
body: I read computer science at Ahram Canadian University, majoring in software engineering, and finished with a 3.36 GPA. The part that shaped how I work was not the coursework — it was the competitive programming community and the year-plus I spent tutoring classmates through data structures, algorithms and project management.

Teaching the same concept to five people who are each stuck at a different point is the fastest way to find out whether you understand it. It is also where I learned that most people are not missing intelligence, they are missing one specific prerequisite nobody went back to fill in. I still write with that in mind.
An honourable mention at the Egyptian Collegiate Programming Contest in 2021 came out of that community rather than anything I did alone.

chapters.title: Shipping for real people before graduating
body: Halfway through the degree I started taking freelance work — websites and small online storefronts, built end to end from static frontends through Django REST Framework APIs and the data behind them.

There was no team, no supervisor and no ticket queue. Scoping a business owner's half-formed idea into something buildable turned out to be most of the job, and it is a skill no coursework had asked me for. It is also the point where 'it works on my machine' stopped being an acceptable end state.

chapters.title: Learning to write software other people maintain
body: At Kites Software I worked on Egypt's first SaaS ERP for import and distribution, building REST endpoints test-first in Java and Spring Boot with Cucumber integration tests against Postgres.

Writing the test before the endpoint felt like a tax for about a week and then stopped feeling like anything at all. Working inside a real Agile cycle — QA finding what I missed, onboarding docs I wrote being used by the next intern — was the first time my code had a life beyond me.

The same year I finished my graduation project, iREAD: a reading platform and digital bookstore serving a Flutter mobile client and a React web client from one REST API, so the business logic had a single home rather than two drifting copies.

chapters.title: Learning to see systems the way an attacker does
body: I spent four months as an offensive security engineer at WE INNOVATE, exploiting web, mobile and infrastructure targets against the OWASP Top 10 and running Active Directory and network penetration tests — every finding documented with a reproducible proof of concept and a remediation path.

Breaking systems for a living permanently changed how I build them. Access control stopped being a UI concern and became a database and API-layer concern. When I later had to resolve a Marketing and Sales data-ownership conflict at EPPS, the answer was obvious in a way it would not have been a year earlier: strip the restricted fields server-side, before the payload ever reaches the client, because anything hidden only in the interface is not hidden at all.

chapters.title: Owning things in production
body: At EPPS I built and now operate an internal B2B lead pipeline replacing spreadsheet tracking across four business entities — roughly 2,000 records, used daily by the eight to ten people running marketing capture through to closed sale. Alongside it: a 3D bin-packing container planner, an IT asset platform tracking about 3,000 assets, and reliability and security across 25+ domains and 7 production sites.
Operating what you build is a different discipline from shipping it. You find out which decisions were convenient and which were correct, usually at an inconvenient hour.

chapters.title: Two products, taken solo from idea to launch
body: Orbit is a professional relationship OS — multi-tenant on Postgres with row-level security, so isolation holds even when the application code above it is wrong. Google OAuth and magic-link auth, Stripe billing with server-side usage metering, Gemini-powered semantic search over your own connections, a D3 force-directed graph, and full English/Arabic RTL as an installable PWA.

Commit is a curriculum tracker for self-taught developers, built around the observation that starting is easy and finishing is not. The whole product speaks git: a study session is a commit, a streak is a contribution graph, finishing a course is merging to main.
Scoping, schema, API, interface, deployment and everything after launch — alone, for both. That is the part I would point at if you asked what I can actually do.

chapters.title: Formalising it
body: I am beginning graduate research in distributed systems and software system design — putting rigour under the parts I learned by building and breaking things.
I write about what I learn on the way, aimed at whoever is one step behind me rather than ten. That audience is easy to help and usually badly served, and I remember being in it.
